newsitem.title: USA: Ex-CIA man pleads guilty to being Moscow spy.
newsitem.headline: Ex-CIA man pleads guilty to being Moscow spy.

text.p: Harold Nicholson, the highest ranking CIA officer convicted of espionage, pleaded guilty on Monday to conspiring to sell highly classified national security secrets to Russia.
In a plea agreement, Nicholson, 46, admitted to spying for Moscow since June 1994, when he was the Central Intelligence Agency's deputy chief of station for operations in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia.

He was the second national security official to cut a deal on charges of selling out their country in three days. On Friday, a former FBI counterintelligence agent, Earl Edwin Pitts, 43, pleaded guilty to selling secrets to Moscow from 1987 to 1992, also in exchange for cash.

Under Nicholson's deal with prosecutors, he could spend as little as 20 years in prison if U.S. officials certify his promised full cooperation in gauging the harm done by his sell-out and if he gets time off for good behaviour.

U.S. District Judge James Cacheris set June 5 for sentencing after ensuring that Nicholson, a 16-year veteran of the CIA's clandestine operations directorate, was entering his plea voluntarily and fully understood the consequences.
Asked whether he knew that he was waiving his right to a jury trial, for instance, Nicholson, in a strong voice betraying no obvious emotion, replied: "I understand that, your honour."

The agreement required Nicholson to forfeit the $180,000 he admitted receiving from Russia's SVRR intelligence service, the successor to the Soviet-era KGB, for the 2 1/2 year conspiracy that ended with his Nov. 16 arrest.

Among the secrets Nicholson admitted selling were the names and planned assignments abroad of new undercover CIA officers he helped train in spycraft at the CIA field school known as Camp Peary, Virginia.

Nicholson also admitted giving Russia a document summarizing information obtained during the debriefing of CIA turncoat Aldrich Ames, who pleaded guilty in 1994 to selling Moscow secrets from 1985 to 1994 for more than $2.5 million.

U.S. officials said Ames's crime led to the deaths of at least 10 Soviet and East European agents secretly in the pay of the United States. Ames was serving a life sentence without possibility of parole.

At one point in the pre-trial manoeuvring, prosecutors dangled the possibility of seeking the death penalty against Nicholson. In espionage cases, capital punishment may be imposed if anyone is killed after being unmasked or if ultra-sensitive nuclear and spy satellite systems are compromised.
U.S. Attorney Helen Fahey, who had overall responsibility for the prosecution, said neither condition for the death penalty had been met in Nicholson's case.
She told a news conference the government's sentencing recommendation hinged on Nicholson's cooperation in reconstructing the secrets he sold to Moscow.

Nicholson still faces a possible maximum sentence of life without parole. But the plea deal binds prosecutors to seek no more than 282 months imprisonment, assuming Nicholson cooperates fully. With a subsequent federally prescribed 15 percent reduction for good behaviour, that means he could be free in 20 years, lawyers said.
Jonathan Shapiro, one of Nicholson's co-lead defence counsels, termed his client, a divorced father of three, "a patriot" who had served his country for 20 years in ways that would never be known.
"What happened in this case was motivated by his loyalty and devotion to family," he said in an interview in his office after the judge accepted Nicholson's plea and pronounced him guilty.
